Less government interference is not always the answer, but increasing competition almost always is. Net Neutrality creates a more competitive environment, specifically under Title II.

Title II requires companies to share infrastructure, meaning that if I were to start an ISP i wouldn't have to build another line of poles next to the competition. There are only so many customers, so at a certain point it is not worth it to build a new network in an already covered neighborhood because the town "ain't big enough for the both of them." By reducing the capital costs, you increase competition. Railroads are required to allow trains from other companies on their tracks in order to avoid redundant infrastructure like that. Utilities have to allow other companies to use their poles and underground conduit. Why shouldn't ISPs?

Plain ol' Net Neutrality is important, too. Imagine if Amazon owned the roads in your town. You could start your own business, but if Amazon feels that you might compete with them, they could charge you more to use their roads (if they allow you at all). Technically you could build your own roads, but even if you could afford it, it would be stupid to build a second road right next to another perfectly good one. You can see how this would kill businesses and decrease competition.

Net Neutrality isn't new, anyway. It was the law until Verizon challenged it a few years ago. The courts said that the FCC could only enforce it if the internet was a Title II utility. The FCC made it one, and that's where we are now. Net Neutrality isn't really "more government" it's the status quo.

Title II requires companies to share infrastructure, meaning that if I were to start an ISP i wouldn't have to build another line of poles next to the competition.
